title: "F-Store — Shared storage with erasure"
status: "Idealized Setup"

*F-Store* (Shared storage with erasure) is part of *Idealized Setup and Resources* in the UC functionality encyclopedia. Status: an idealized setup assumption or shared resource.

*F-Rand*'s companion: where a randomness source produces values and lets them be forgotten, a store takes values and holds them until they are. A party puts a value at an index, gets it back, and can erase it; an erased index is reusable. Together the two are what lets a protocol keep no persistent state on its own machine tape — draw coins through *F-Rand*, keep everything else through *F-Store* — so that whatever the adversary can read off a corrupt party's leakage is exactly what these two functionalities choose to expose, and nothing hidden in an implementation's memory besides.

## Functionality

State: a table $\mathtt{L} : \mathbb{N} \to \{0,1\}^* \cup \{\bot, \square\}$, initially $\mathtt{L}[*] = \square$. An index is in one of three conditions, kept deliberately distinct: $\square$ if nothing was ever put there, a value if put and not erased, and $\bot$ if put and then erased — so a caller can tell "nothing was ever here" from "something was here and is gone," rather than a store that answers the same either way and cannot be asked whether an erasure actually happened.

- **Put(i, x)**: requires $\mathtt{L}[i] \in \{\bot, \square\}$ (an occupied index refuses); sets $\mathtt{L}[i] \gets x$ and returns $\mathsf{ok}$.
- **Erase(i)**: sets $\mathtt{L}[i] \gets \bot$ and returns $\mathsf{ok}$ — erasing an index that holds nothing is a harmless no-op.
- **Get(i)**: requires $\mathtt{L}[i] \neq \square$ (never written refuses); returns $\mathtt{L}[i]$, which is $\bot$ if the entry was erased.
- **Leak()**: returns $\mathtt{L}$ in full.

State is shared across every party the instance serves, exactly as for *F-Rand*: one party may retrieve what another put, which is what makes it a shared store rather than a per-party tape.

Below is the functionality itself, transcribed from [*UC for Gamers*](/surveys/uc-for-gamers/pdf/main.pdf#page=141) (§14.1, p. 140), line numbering and all. Two markers do the work of three conditions: $\square$ is never written, $\bot$ is written and since erased, and anything else is a value put and still there. The refusals are written as **require**s rather than as returns of $\mathsf{rej}$ — the framework answers a refused **require** with $\mathsf{rej}$, so lines 3 and 8 are exactly the two refusals a store owes.

```{=html}
<div class="cj-interface">
<div class="cj-interface-head">
<div class="cj-interface-title">Functionality \(\mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{Store}}\)</div>
<div class="cj-interface-params">\(\mathit{pid}\), &nbsp; \(\mathbf{P}\), &nbsp; \(\mathbf{N}\), &nbsp; \(\mathbf{U} := \emptyset\), &nbsp; \(\mathit{par} := \bot\)</div>
</div>
<div class="cj-interface-body">

<div class="cj-op">
<div class="cj-op-sig">Initialize():</div>
<ol class="cj-code" start="1">
<li>\(\mathtt{L} : \mathbb{N} \to \{0,1\}^{*} \cup \{\bot, \square\}\)</li>
<li>\(\mathtt{L}[*] \gets \square\)</li>
</ol>
</div>

<div class="cj-op">
<div class="cj-op-sig"><span class="cj-id">id</span>.Put(<span class="cj-id">i</span>, <span class="cj-id">x</span>)<span class="cj-op-from">from <span class="cj-id">id</span>′</span></div>
<ol class="cj-code" start="3">
<li>\(\textbf{require}\ \mathtt{L}[i] \in \{\bot, \square\}\)<span class="cj-comment">// an occupied index refuses</span></li>
<li>\(\mathtt{L}[i] \gets x\)</li>
<li>\(\textbf{return}\)&nbsp;<span class="cj-atom">ok</span></li>
</ol>
</div>

<div class="cj-op">
<div class="cj-op-sig"><span class="cj-id">id</span>.Erase(<span class="cj-id">i</span>)<span class="cj-op-from">from <span class="cj-id">id</span>′</span></div>
<ol class="cj-code" start="6">
<li>\(\mathtt{L}[i] \gets \bot\)</li>
<li>\(\textbf{return}\)&nbsp;<span class="cj-atom">ok</span></li>
</ol>
</div>

<div class="cj-op">
<div class="cj-op-sig"><span class="cj-id">id</span>.Get(<span class="cj-id">i</span>)<span class="cj-op-from">from <span class="cj-id">id</span>′</span></div>
<ol class="cj-code" start="8">
<li>\(\textbf{require}\ \mathtt{L}[i] \neq \square\)<span class="cj-comment">// never written refuses</span></li>
<li>\(\textbf{return}\ \mathtt{L}[i]\)<span class="cj-comment">// \(\bot\) if erased</span></li>
</ol>
</div>

<div class="cj-op">
<div class="cj-op-sig"><span class="cj-id">id</span>.Leak()<span class="cj-op-from">from <span class="cj-id">id</span>′</span></div>
<ol class="cj-code" start="10">
<li>\(\textbf{return}\ \mathtt{L}\)</li>
</ol>
</div>

</div>
</div>
```

## Known realizations

An idealization of ordinary local storage together with a secure-erasure primitive; nothing computational realizes the erasure guarantee exactly, since a real machine's memory is not erasure-transparent the way this functionality's $\mathsf{gone}$ marker is. It stands in, in a protocol write-up, for "this value is kept on the party's own tape until explicitly deleted."

## Properties

Two properties, proven with probability exactly $0$ (information-theoretic, no adversary strategy succeeds at all):

- **Persistence.** A value put and not erased is the value later got back — no get ever returns anything other than the last successful put at that index, so long as no erasure intervened.
- **Erasure.** A value that has been erased is never got back — no get ever returns the value an erasure removed, so long as no later put restored it first.

Both hold against every occupant of the adversary slot, not just a canonical one, since (as with *F-Rand*) the functionality places no calls of its own for an adversary to interfere with.
